newsitem.title: BOTSWANA: Botswana budget should focus on pula-rand ties.
newsitem.headline: Botswana budget should focus on pula-rand ties.

text.p: Diamond-rich Botswana's 1997/98 budget should focus on a weakening pula and better incentives for foreign investment, analysts said.

The budget, to be unveiled on Monday, is once again expected to show a surplus. Finance Minister Festus Mogae told Reuters in December he expected Botswana to record its 15th consecutive surplus in 1997/98, thanks to higher pula diamond revenues.

Botswana is well on course for a surplus in the current 1996/97 budget year ending in March, despite initial forecasts of a 636 million pula ($178 million) shortfall, reflecting windfall profits in pula terms on the country's dollar reserves.

The pula -- which shadows South Africa's rand -- stood at 35 U.S. cents at the start of 1996 but had fallen to 27 cents by the end of the December. This year it has strengthened only slightly to 28 cents, despite the strong rally in the rand.
Standard Chartered's managing director in Botswana, Les Gibson, said Mogae should explain why the pula had been allowed to slip against the rand.
"There was reason for the pula to drop with the rand, but a three percent drift down against the rand over the last few weeks is puzzling," Gibson told Reuters.
On the tax front, Alan Norrie, acting chairman and chief executive officer of the Botswana Stock Exchange, predicted cuts in personal taxes as well as a widening of tax bands.
"My guess is that the top rate of personal tax will come down to 25 per cent (from 30 per cent) to match company tax," he said.
"We have had quite a substantial inflationary devaluation of the pula as it has gone down with the rand.

"One way to alleviate that and put money back into people's pockets in an non-inflationary way is a lower marginal tax rate to prevent pay increases taking salaries straight into the top brackets," he added.
Norrie said he hoped to see more company tax incentives such as accelerated write-offs for capital expenditure.
"At the moment if you put a building up in Botswana, it takes 25 years to write it off," he said.
Norrie said tax on overseas earnings could be introduced as a precursor to the total abolition of exchange controls.
Although he believes this will not happen this year, he does however see substantial further liberalisation of Botswana's exchange controls.
Barclays Bank managing director Charles Middleton told Reuters he hoped for better investor incentives.
"There are still opportunities to make Botswana a more attractive place for investors," he said.
Middleton believes worthwhile development projects are not being implemented.
"It is important that the private sector encourages the government to take things forward," he said. "A lot of good ideas are coming out of government. They must be pushed through more aggressively."
He said the government should concentrate on offering better incentives to small business to help lower unemployment, which affects nearly 30 percent of the workforce.
"It is imperative that there is growth in that sector," Middleton said.
This could be achieved through a revitalisation of the Trade and Industry Promotion Agency (TIPA), he said..
Peter Dart, finance director for Standard Chartered Bank, said foreign exchange policy was a burning issue for foreign investors: "The policy of tying the pula to the rand needs to be clarified."
